events.title: Accession of Tiberius
events.summary: Already holding tribunician power and proconsular imperium, Tiberius gave the watchword to the praetorians at once on Augustus's death, but in the Senate staged a long show of reluctance before accepting the position, likening it to holding a wolf by the ears.
events.detail: Tacitus dramatises the debate: Asinius Gallus asked which part of the state Tiberius wanted, Quintus Haterius asked how long he would leave the state without a head, and Mamercus Scaurus hoped his refusal would not be vetoed with his tribunician power. Tiberius claimed he would accept until the senators judged it right to give him rest in old age. The episode is the first transfer of power in the Principate and shows that no constitutional mechanism of succession existed; Tacitus reads it as hypocrisy, modern scholars often as genuine uncertainty about forms.

events.title: Murder of Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus's last surviving grandson was killed on Planasia by a centurion immediately after Augustus's death: 'the first crime of the new principate', in Tacitus's phrase. Tiberius denied responsibility; the order may have come from Augustus, Livia or Sallustius Crispus.
events.detail: In AD 16 a slave of Postumus named Clemens, who resembled him, impersonated his dead master, gathered followers in Etruria and Gaul and even in Rome before being captured and executed in the palace; asked how he had become Agrippa, he reportedly answered 'as you became Caesar'.

events.title: Mutinies of the Pannonian and German legions
events.summary: On news of Augustus's death the three Pannonian legions and the four legions of the lower Rhine mutinied, demanding service limited to 16 years, a denarius a day in pay and discharge bonuses in cash in camp. Drusus quelled the Pannonian mutiny, Germanicus the German one.
events.detail: In Pannonia the ex-claqueur Percennius and the soldier Vibulenus led the movement; a lunar eclipse during the night of 26/27 September AD 14 (astronomically confirmed) terrified the soldiers and helped Drusus regain control. On the Rhine, at Ara Ubiorum, mutineers offered Germanicus the throne; when he drew his sword to kill himself one soldier offered his own as 'sharper'. Sending away his pregnant wife Agrippina and little son 'Caligula' shamed the troops, who then massacred their own ringleaders at Vetera. Germanicus led them across the Rhine to expiate their guilt. Tacitus's speeches for the mutineers (Ann. 1.17) are a rare articulation of soldiers' grievances: beatings by centurions, extortion for leave, being paid 10 asses a day for their bodies and souls.
events.locName: Ara Ubiorum (Cologne) and Pannonian summer camp

events.title: Elections transferred from the people to the Senate
events.summary: In the first year of Tiberius the election of magistrates passed effectively from the popular assemblies to the Senate, which drew up lists that the comitia merely ratified. Tacitus says the people, apart from idle murmurs, did not complain.
events.detail: Tiberius commended four of the twelve praetorian candidates, who had to be elected. The procedure of destinatio by special centuries of senators and equites (named after Gaius and Lucius under the lex Valeria Cornelia of AD 5 and expanded for Germanicus and Drusus), known from the Tabula Hebana and Tabula Siarensis, had already narrowed the field. The comitia met for a ceremonial renuntiatio into the third century.
scholarship: Levick, 'Imperial control of the elections under the early Principate', Historia 16 (1967)

events.title: Germanicus's massacre of the Marsi
events.summary: To channel the guilt of the mutiny, Germanicus led 12,000 legionaries, 26 auxiliary cohorts and 8 alae across the Rhine and fell on the Marsi during a nocturnal festival, killing without distinction of age or sex over fifty miles and razing their most famous shrine, of the goddess Tanfana.
events.detail: The Bructeri, Tubantes and Usipetes ambushed the returning column in the forest but were beaten off by the twentieth legion. Tanfana is otherwise unknown. The raid was a punitive gesture rather than a campaign of conquest.
events.locName: Territory of the Marsi, between Lippe and Ruhr

battle.significance: First act of the campaigns of revenge for Varus.

events.title: Battle of Pontes Longi
events.summary: Returning from the Varian battlefield across the causeways called 'long bridges' through the moors, Caecina's four legions were caught by Arminius in a marsh and nearly suffered Varus's fate; they were saved when the Germans, against Arminius's advice, assaulted the fortified camp and were routed by a sally.
events.detail: Tacitus says Caecina dreamt that Varus rose from the swamp and beckoned him. Panic in the camp at night was stopped by Caecina lying across the gate. A rumour that the army was lost nearly led to the destruction of the Rhine bridge at Vetera, which Agrippina personally prevented, distributing clothing and dressings to the returning wounded. Earlier that summer Lucius Stertinius recovered the eagle of legio XIX from the Bructeri, and Germanicus buried the Varian dead, laying the first sod of their mound.
events.locName: Pontes longi, moors between Ems and Rhine

battle.significance: A narrow escape that revealed the vulnerability of Roman columns in the north German plain.

events.title: Trial of Libo Drusus
events.summary: Marcus Scribonius Libo Drusus, a young noble related to Pompey and the Julii, was accused of plotting revolution on the evidence of consultations with astrologers, magicians and dream-interpreters; he committed suicide during the trial, and his estate was divided among the accusers.
events.detail: It was the first great maiestas trial of the reign, with informers rewarded from the accused's property. The Senate expelled astrologers and magicians from Italy, executing two. The Fasti Amiternini and Antiates mark 13 September as a holiday because on that day Libo's 'nefaria consilia' were condemned. Tacitus presents it as the beginning of the 'evil that would devour the state'.

events.title: Battle of Idistaviso
events.summary: On a plain called Idistaviso between the Weser and the hills, Germanicus's eight legions and auxiliaries crushed Arminius's Cherusci in a set-piece battle; the Germans were driven into the river and forest and slaughtered over ten miles.
events.detail: Before the battle Germanicus walked through the camp in disguise to hear the soldiers' mood, and eight eagles flying into the forest were taken as an omen for the eight legions. Arminius escaped by smearing his face with his own blood; his uncle Inguiomerus also got away. The soldiers hailed Tiberius imperator and raised a trophy of captured arms. Days earlier Arminius had argued across the Weser with his brother Flavus, a Roman officer who had lost an eye in Roman service, a famous scene in Tacitus.
events.locName: Idistaviso, on the Weser near Minden or Rinteln

sides.strength: 8 legions with auxiliaries, Batavian cavalry and archers: c. 70,000

battle.significance: Avenged Varus in the field but did not destroy Arminius's power.

events.title: Battle of the Angrivarian Wall
events.summary: Weeks after Idistaviso, the Germans made a stand behind the boundary earthwork between the Angrivarii and Cherusci; Germanicus stormed it with slingers and artillery, fought bareheaded so as to be recognised, and ordered that no prisoners be taken.
events.detail: Afterwards he set up a trophy inscribed that the army of Tiberius Caesar, having subdued the nations between Rhine and Elbe, dedicated the monument to Mars, Jupiter and Augustus, without mentioning himself. On the way home much of the fleet was destroyed in a North Sea storm; survivors told tales of sea monsters and bird-men. Tiberius then recalled Germanicus to a triumph, saying the Germans could be left to their own quarrels.

battle.significance: Last major Roman battle in free Germany for two centuries before Maximinus Thrax's campaign (the Harzhorn, c. 235).

events.title: Triumph of Germanicus
events.summary: Germanicus triumphed over the Cherusci, Chatti, Angrivarii and other peoples as far as the Elbe, with his five children in the chariot. Among the captives was Thusnelda, Arminius's wife, with their three-year-old son Thumelicus, born in captivity.
events.detail: Strabo, writing at the time, lists the captives, including Thusnelda's brother Segimundus and the Chattan priest Libes, and notes that Thusnelda's father Segestes watched as an honoured guest. An arch near the temple of Saturn commemorated the recovery of the Varian standards. The war was officially over, but only two of the three eagles had been recovered; the third came back in 41.

events.title: Annexation of Cappadocia and Commagene
events.summary: King Archelaus of Cappadocia, summoned to Rome and accused before the Senate, died there; Tiberius annexed his kingdom under an equestrian procurator. Commagene, after the death of Antiochus III, was attached to Syria in the same year.
events.detail: Tiberius used the new revenues to halve the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium) that funded the military treasury. Germanicus was sent east with imperium maius to organise the new provinces and settle Armenia. Commagene was restored as a kingdom to Antiochus IV by Caligula in 38 and finally annexed in 72. Archelaus's offence, Tacitus says, was having neglected Tiberius during his retirement on Rhodes.

events.title: Great earthquake in Asia
events.summary: In one night an earthquake destroyed twelve cities of Asia, Sardis worst of all. Tiberius gave Sardis 10 million sesterces and remitted the tribute of the affected cities for five years.
events.detail: Pliny calls it the greatest earthquake in human memory. A senator of praetorian rank was sent to oversee reconstruction. A statue base found at Puteoli (CIL X 1624), dedicated to Tiberius in 30 by the Augustales, carries relief personifications of fourteen Asian cities, the twelve of 17 plus Cibyra and Ephesus, damaged in later quakes (23, 29), probably copying a monument in Rome. Coins of Tiberius with CIVITATIBVS ASIAE RESTITVTIS celebrate the relief.

events.title: Germanicus in the East and his visit to Egypt
events.summary: Germanicus crowned Zeno, son of Polemon of Pontus, as Artaxias III of Armenia at Artaxata in 18, organised Cappadocia and Commagene, and in early 19 toured Egypt, sailing up the Nile to Thebes and Syene, without the emperor's permission that Augustus required of senators.
events.detail: At Alexandria he opened the state granaries to relieve a famine. A papyrus (P.Oxy. XXV 2435) records his speech to the Alexandrians and an edict (SB I 3924) rejects divine acclamations as appropriate only to Tiberius and Livia. Tiberius rebuked him for both his dress and his entry into Egypt. Throughout, he feuded with Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, governor of Syria, and his wife Plancina, whom many believed Tiberius had placed to check him.

events.title: Death of Germanicus
events.summary: Germanicus died at Epidaphne near Antioch, aged 33, convinced that Piso and Plancina had poisoned him. Remains of human bodies, spells and lead tablets inscribed with his name were found hidden in his house.
events.detail: His body was exhibited in the forum of Antioch; some saw signs of poison. Agrippina carried his ashes to Brundisium and Rome amid vast public mourning; Suetonius says temples were stoned, household gods thrown into the street, and even the Parthian king suspended his hunting. Tiberius and Livia did not appear in public. The death left Tiberius's son Drusus as heir and deepened the rift between Tiberius and Agrippina's family. Tacitus's comparison of Germanicus with Alexander the Great is a deliberate set piece.

events.title: Senatorial honours for Germanicus (Tabula Siarensis and Tabula Hebana)
events.summary: The Senate decreed posthumous honours for Germanicus in December 19, including marble arches in the Circus Flaminius, on the Rhine near Drusus's cenotaph at Mainz, and on Mount Amanus in Syria. Bronze copies found in Spain (Tabula Siarensis, 1982) and Etruria (Tabula Hebana, 1947) preserve the decree and the resulting law.
events.detail: The Tabula Hebana records the creation of five new 'centuries of Germanicus' in the destinatio assembly that pre-selected consuls and praetors, showing how electoral procedure had been engineered. The texts allow direct comparison with Tacitus's summary (Ann. 2.83), which proves accurate though selective. They also show the dissemination of senatorial decrees to provincial towns as part of dynastic loyalism.
scholarship: González, 'Tabula Siarensis, Fortunales Siarenses et municipia civium Romanorum', ZPE 55 (1984)

events.title: Expulsion of Jews and worshippers of Isis from Rome
events.summary: A senatus consultum banished Egyptian and Jewish rites from Rome; 4,000 freedmen 'tainted with that superstition' were drafted to Sardinia to fight bandits, and the rest ordered to leave Italy unless they renounced their rites.
events.detail: Josephus attributes the measures to two scandals: a noblewoman, Paulina, seduced in the temple of Isis by an equestrian posing as Anubis with the priests' connivance (the priests were crucified and the temple razed), and a convert, Fulvia, defrauded of gifts for the Jerusalem Temple. Tacitus remarks that if the conscripts died of the climate in Sardinia it would be 'a cheap loss'. The same year astrologers were again expelled.

events.title: Trial of Piso and the Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre
events.summary: Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, accused of poisoning Germanicus and of attempting to retake his province by force after being dismissed, was tried before the Senate and killed himself before the verdict. The Senate's resulting decree, dated 10 December 20, survives in several bronze copies from Baetica.
events.detail: The decree, found near Seville in the late 1980s and published in 1996, condemns Piso's memory, confiscates part of his estate, orders his name erased from a statue of Germanicus, pardons his wife Plancina at Livia's request, and praises the loyalty of the soldiers and the restraint of the imperial family. It does not uphold the poisoning charge. It is the longest senatus consultum on record and confirms that Tacitus used senatorial records (acta senatus), though it shows he compressed and dramatised; the date of the decree also shows that Tacitus's sequence of events is slightly off.
events.locName: Rome (copies found at El Tejar, Seville)
scholarship: Eck, Caballos and Fernández, Das senatus consultum de Cn. Pisone patre (1996)

events.title: Revolt of Florus and Sacrovir; battle near Augustodunum
events.summary: Indebted Gallic notables rose under the Treveran Julius Florus and the Aeduan Julius Sacrovir, both Roman citizens. Florus was defeated in the Ardennes by a fellow-Treveran; Sacrovir seized Augustodunum and its schools of noble youths, but his army was crushed by Gaius Silius twelve miles from the city.
events.detail: Sacrovir's 40,000 men included a fifth equipped with legionary arms and a corps of crupellarii, slave gladiators encased in iron armour, whom the legionaries cut down with axes and picks 'as if demolishing a wall'. Sacrovir and his companions burned themselves in a villa. Tacitus ascribes the revolt to debts, tribute and the harshness of governors; Velleius blames Sacrovir alone. Tiberius did not leave Rome, a point of criticism.

sides.strength: 2 legions of upper Germany with auxiliaries

battle.significance: The last significant revolt in central Gaul until 68-70.

events.title: Death of Arminius
events.summary: Arminius, after defeating his rival Maroboduus in 17 and seeing him expelled to Roman exile, was killed by his own kinsmen for aspiring to kingship, aged 37, after twelve years of power.
events.detail: Tacitus's obituary calls him 'without doubt the liberator of Germany' and notes that he was still celebrated in German songs; he records that the Chattan chief Adgandestrius had offered to poison him, and that Tiberius proudly refused, preferring open arms. Maroboduus, overthrown by Catualda in 18-19, lived for 18 years at Ravenna. Arminius's son Thumelicus was raised at Ravenna and met an undisclosed fate.

events.title: Death of Drusus the Younger
events.summary: Tiberius's only son and designated successor, who had held the tribunician power since 22, died apparently of illness. Eight years later Sejanus's divorced wife Apicata revealed that Drusus had been poisoned by Sejanus and Drusus's wife Livilla, using the eunuch Lygdus.
events.detail: Tacitus presents the death as the turning point of the reign and accepts the poisoning story while rejecting a further rumour that Tiberius himself gave Drusus the cup. With Drusus dead, Tiberius commended Germanicus's sons Nero and Drusus to the Senate, setting Sejanus against Agrippina's family. Drusus's twin sons were born in 19; one, Tiberius Gemellus, survived.
events.debate: The poison story rests on Apicata's testimony, given in grief after her children's execution, and on confessions under torture.

events.title: Sejanus concentrates the praetorians in the Castra Praetoria
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Lucius Aelius Sejanus brought the praetorian cohorts, previously billeted in and around Rome, into a single fortified camp on the north-eastern edge of the city, making them a concentrated political force.
events.detail: The camp (about 440 by 380 m) on the Viminal had brick-faced concrete walls, one of the earliest large uses of brick facing in Rome; Aurelian later incorporated its north, east and south walls into the city wall, where they can still be seen. From here the praetorians would make and unmake emperors, beginning with Claudius in 41.

events.title: Battle of Auzea and death of Tacfarinas
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella, with help from king Ptolemy of Mauretania, located Tacfarinas's camp beside the half-ruined fort of Auzea, surrounded it with light columns and attacked at dawn, killing Tacfarinas, who threw himself on the Roman weapons, and ending the seven-year war.
events.detail: Tacfarinas's son was captured and his brother escaped. The Senate denied Dolabella triumphal ornaments to protect the reputation of Junius Blaesus, uncle of Sejanus; Tacitus regards this as discreditable. Ptolemy was rewarded with an ivory sceptre and embroidered toga, the old honours for a friend of the Roman people.

sides.strength: Legio III Augusta, auxiliaries and Mauretanian cavalry

battle.significance: Ended the longest guerrilla war of Tiberius's reign.

events.title: Trial of Cremutius Cordus
events.summary: The historian Aulus Cremutius Cordus was prosecuted by clients of Sejanus for having praised Brutus and called Cassius 'the last of the Romans' in his histories. After a defiant speech he starved himself to death, and the Senate ordered his books burned.
events.detail: Tacitus gives him a speech defending freedom of historical judgement and comments that the punishment of talent only increases its authority. His daughter Marcia preserved copies, and the work was republished under Caligula; Seneca's Consolation to Marcia praises her for it. The case is a landmark in the history of literary censorship.

events.title: Revolt of the Thracian hill tribes
events.summary: Thracian mountain peoples, refusing to supply recruits to Roman units and serve far from home, rebelled against the client king Rhoemetalces II; Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus, governor of Moesia, blockaded them in a fortress on the Haemus until thirst and disease forced surrender.
events.detail: Tacitus's detailed account shows the role of client-kingdom levies in the Roman army and Roman tactics of circumvallation in mountainous country. Poppaeus Sabinus received triumphal ornaments. Thrace was annexed in 46.

events.title: Tiberius withdraws from Rome to Capri
events.summary: Tiberius left Rome for Campania in 26 and in 27 settled on Capri, never to return to the city; he governed by letter, leaving Sejanus as the indispensable intermediary.
events.detail: At Spelunca (Sperlonga) the roof of a seaside grotto where he was dining collapsed, and Sejanus shielded him with his body, earning his total trust; the grotto, excavated in 1957, yielded the colossal Odysseus sculpture groups by Rhodian sculptors. On Capri Tiberius built or enlarged twelve villas, of which the Villa Jovis on the eastern cliffs survives. Suetonius's catalogue of his vices there derives from hostile gossip.

events.title: Collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae
events.summary: A wooden amphitheatre built on poor foundations by a freedman named Atilius, to profit from gladiatorial shows, collapsed at Fidenae near Rome during a crowded spectacle. Tacitus gives 50,000 killed or injured, Suetonius 20,000 killed.
events.detail: The Senate responded with safety rules: no one with less than 400,000 sesterces could put on gladiatorial games, and amphitheatres were to be built only on ground tested for soundness. Atilius was exiled. Rich houses were opened to the injured, and Tacitus compares the scene to a battle.

events.title: Revolt of the Frisii and battle of Baduhenna Wood
events.summary: The Frisii, whose tribute of ox-hides had been arbitrarily redefined by the primipilaris Olennius as hides of aurochs size, hanged the Roman soldiers collecting it and besieged the fort of Flevum. In the relief operations under Lucius Apronius, 900 Romans were cut down in the sacred wood of Baduhenna.
events.detail: A further 400 who had occupied the villa of a former auxiliary named Cruptorix killed one another rather than fall into Frisian hands. Tiberius concealed the losses to avoid entrusting a war to anyone, and the Frisii remained independent until Corbulo's operations of 47. Tacitus says their name then became famous among the Germans.

sides.strength: Vexillations of the lower German legions and auxiliaries
sides.losses: c. 1,300 (900 in the wood, 400 at Cruptorix's villa)

battle.significance: Showed the cost of arbitrary tribute and the weakness of Rome's hold beyond the Rhine delta.

events.title: Death of Livia
events.summary: Livia (Julia Augusta) died aged 86. Tiberius did not attend the funeral, vetoed her deification and ignored her will; her great-grandson Gaius (Caligula), aged 17, delivered the eulogy.
events.detail: Tacitus marks her death as removing the last restraint on Tiberius and Sejanus: 'from then on it was sheer, oppressive despotism'. The Senate voted an arch, which Tiberius promised to build himself and never did. Claudius deified her in 42. Her villa at Prima Porta, with its garden fresco room and the Augustus statue, survives.

events.title: Destruction of Agrippina the Elder and her sons
events.summary: A letter from Tiberius denounced Agrippina and her eldest son Nero Caesar; she was exiled to Pandateria and he to Pontia, where he died in 31. Her second son Drusus Caesar was imprisoned in the palace and starved to death in 33; Agrippina starved herself on 18 October 33, two years to the day after Sejanus's fall.
events.detail: Tacitus says Drusus was reduced to chewing the stuffing of his mattress and that Tiberius had the daily record of his words and sufferings, kept by a guard, read out in the Senate. Only the youngest son, Gaius, survived on Capri with Tiberius. Agrippina had lost an eye to a centurion's beating. Tiberius later boasted that he had not had her strangled.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus of Nazareth, a Galilean Jewish preacher and healer, was crucified in Jerusalem around Passover on the order of the prefect Pontius Pilate. Tacitus, the only pagan author to mention it explicitly, records that 'Christus, the author of the name, was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilatus in the reign of Tiberius'.
events.detail: The year is either 30 or 33, the two in which Passover-eve could fall on a Friday consistent with the Gospels. Pilate's existence and title (praefectus, not procurator as Tacitus anachronistically says) are confirmed by the 'Pilate Stone' found at Caesarea in 1961, recording his dedication of a Tiberieum. Josephus's Testimonium Flavianum (AJ 18.63-64) is generally held to be partly authentic but Christianised. Pilate was removed in 36/37 by the Syrian legate Lucius Vitellius after massacring Samaritans at Mount Gerizim.
scholarship: Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus (1993)
events.debate: Date (30 vs 33); authenticity of the Testimonium Flavianum; division of responsibility between Pilate and the Temple authorities.

events.title: Fall of Sejanus
events.summary: At the height of his power, consul with Tiberius and betrothed into the imperial family, Sejanus was destroyed by a long letter from Capri read to the Senate. The new praetorian prefect Macro had secured the guard, and Sejanus was executed the same day and his body thrown down the Gemonian stairs.
events.detail: Josephus says Antonia, Tiberius's sister-in-law, alerted the emperor by a letter carried by her freedman Pallas. The vigiles under Graecinius Laco replaced the praetorians around the Senate. Sejanus's statues were smashed (Juvenal's tenth satire makes them into chamber pots). His young children were executed, his daughter raped by the executioner beforehand because it was unlawful to execute a virgin; his former wife Apicata killed herself after denouncing the poisoning of Drusus. A wave of prosecutions of his associates followed. The portion of Tacitus's Annals narrating the fall is lost, so Dio's account (58.9-11) is central.

events.title: Credit crisis of AD 33
events.summary: Prosecutions under a neglected Caesarian law requiring creditors to invest a share of their capital in Italian land triggered a scramble to call in loans, a collapse of land prices and a liquidity crisis in Rome. Tiberius made 100 million sesterces available through banks as three-year interest-free loans secured on land worth double.
events.detail: The Senate first gave lenders 18 months to comply and ordered two-thirds of loans to be invested in Italian land, but debtors had to sell to repay, flooding the market. The episode is an unusually detailed ancient account of credit contraction and a state bailout; it has attracted modern economic historians since Tenney Frank (1935).
scholarship: Frank, 'The financial crisis of 33 A.D.', AJP 56 (1935)
Rodewald, Money in the Age of Tiberius (1976)

events.title: Death of Tiberius
events.summary: Tiberius died at the villa of Lucullus at Misenum, aged 77. Tacitus reports that when he unexpectedly revived after being thought dead, Macro had him smothered with bedclothes; Suetonius gives versions blaming Caligula.
events.detail: The Roman crowd reportedly shouted 'Tiberius to the Tiber!'. His will made Gaius and his grandson Tiberius Gemellus co-heirs, but the Senate annulled it. Tacitus's character sketch traces Tiberius's decline in stages as each restraint (Germanicus, Drusus, Livia, Sejanus) disappeared, a famous and much criticised schema.

events.title: Accession of Gaius (Caligula)
events.summary: The Senate conferred all the powers of the principate on the 24-year-old Gaius in a single session, setting aside Tiberius's will that had made Gemellus co-heir. He entered Rome on 28 March to wild popular enthusiasm as the son of Germanicus.
events.detail: Suetonius says more than 160,000 victims were sacrificed in thanksgiving in three months. Gaius brought back the ashes of his mother and brother from the islands, recalled exiles, published imperial accounts, restored elections to the people (briefly) and paid Tiberius's legacies. The one-day conferral of powers, rather than piecemeal grants as for Augustus and Tiberius, foreshadows the later lex de imperio.

events.title: Caligula's illness and the first purges
events.summary: In October 37 Gaius fell gravely ill; after recovering he forced Tiberius Gemellus to kill himself, then destroyed his father-in-law Marcus Junius Silanus and Macro, the prefect who had helped him to power.
events.detail: Philo, writing a few years later, saw the illness as the turning point after seven months of exemplary government; modern scholars dispute whether it caused any mental change or simply freed him from his early backers. People who had vowed their lives for his recovery were held to their vows.

events.title: Anti-Jewish riots in Alexandria
events.summary: After the Jewish king Agrippa I passed through Alexandria and was mocked by a Greek mob dressing up a madman named Carabas as a king, the prefect Avillius Flaccus allowed images of the emperor to be placed in synagogues, declared Jews foreigners and confined them to one quarter, where many were killed.
events.detail: Flaccus was arrested in October 38 and exiled to Andros, where he was later executed. Rival Jewish and Greek embassies, led by Philo and by Apion, went to Gaius in 39/40; Philo's Legatio ad Gaium describes a farcical audience in the gardens of Maecenas. Claudius's letter to the Alexandrians (41) settled the dispute. Philo's In Flaccum is our main source and is intensely partisan; the conflict turned on Jewish claims to civic rights in Alexandria.
scholarship: Gruen, Diaspora: Jews amidst Greeks and Romans (2002)

events.title: Death and deification of Drusilla
events.summary: Gaius's favourite sister Julia Drusilla died; on 23 September 38 the Senate consecrated her as Diva Drusilla, the first Roman woman to be deified.
events.detail: A senator, Livius Geminius, swore he had seen her ascend to heaven and was paid a million sesterces. She had been named heir to Gaius's property and power in his illness of 37. Ancient allegations of incest between Gaius and his sisters are generally viewed with scepticism. Her cult as Panthea was short-lived.

events.title: Conspiracy of Gaetulicus and Lepidus
events.summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus, commander of upper Germany for ten years, and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Drusilla's widower, were executed for an alleged plot; Gaius's sisters Agrippina and Livilla were exiled, Agrippina made to carry Lepidus's ashes to Rome.
events.detail: The Arval Brethren recorded sacrifices on 27 October 39 'for the detection of the wicked plots of Gnaeus Lentulus Gaetulicus against Gaius Germanicus' (CIL VI 32346). Gaius had marched north with praetorians before the plot broke, and Servius Sulpicius Galba replaced Gaetulicus. Vespasian, as praetor, moved that the conspirators be denied burial.

events.title: Caligula's German and British expedition
events.summary: Gaius spent the winter of 39/40 on the Rhine and the Channel coast, staged punitive raids across the Rhine, accepted the surrender of the British prince Adminius, and, according to Suetonius, ordered his troops drawn up on the shore to gather seashells as 'spoils of the Ocean'.
events.detail: He built a lighthouse at Gesoriacum (the Tour d'Ordre, standing until 1644). The seashell story has been rationalised by modern scholars, who suggest that 'musculi' meant engineers' huts or that the troops refused to embark; preparations he made may have facilitated Claudius's invasion three years later. He celebrated an ovatio in Rome on his birthday, 31 August 40.
events.debate: The seashells: lunacy, mockery of mutinous troops, or misunderstanding of a technical term.

events.title: Murder of Ptolemy and annexation of Mauretania
events.summary: Gaius summoned his cousin Ptolemy, king of Mauretania and grandson of Antony and Cleopatra, and had him killed, allegedly because his purple cloak drew admiration at the games or because of his wealth. The kingdom was annexed, provoking a revolt led by Ptolemy's freedman Aedemon.
events.detail: The revolt took two years to suppress (Suetonius Paullinus crossed the Atlas in 42; Hosidius Geta pursued the Moorish leader Salabus into the desert). Claudius divided the territory into two procuratorial provinces, Mauretania Caesariensis (capital Iol Caesarea) and Tingitana (capital Tingis). An inscription from Volubilis honours Marcus Valerius Severus, who commanded auxiliaries against Aedemon and obtained Roman citizenship and municipal status for the town.

events.title: Caligula's statue for the Jerusalem Temple
events.summary: After Jews of Jamnia tore down an altar erected to the emperor by local Greeks, Gaius ordered the legate of Syria, Publius Petronius, to install a colossal statue of himself as Zeus in the Temple of Jerusalem. Petronius delayed in the face of mass non-violent protest; Agrippa I interceded; Gaius's death ended the crisis.
events.detail: Josephus describes tens of thousands of Jews at Ptolemais and Tiberias who lay on the ground for forty days, abandoning the sowing, and declared they would die rather than see the Temple profaned. Gaius ordered Petronius to commit suicide, but the letter arrived after news of the emperor's assassination. Tacitus (Hist. 5.9) says the Jews took up arms rather than accept the order. The episode left a deep mark on Jewish and early Christian apocalyptic thought.

events.title: Assassination of Caligula
events.summary: During the Palatine Games, Gaius was stabbed to death in a covered passage of the palace by the praetorian tribune Cassius Chaerea, whom he had repeatedly mocked with obscene watchwords, together with Cornelius Sabinus and other officers. His wife Caesonia and infant daughter were killed soon after.
events.detail: The conspiracy reached senators, the prefects and imperial freedmen. While the Senate debated restoring the Republic on the Capitol, praetorians looting the palace found Gaius's uncle Claudius hiding behind a curtain and carried him to their camp. Josephus's long account (AJ 19.1-273), probably drawn from a Roman eyewitness source such as Cluvius Rufus, is the fullest narrative of any imperial assassination. Gaius was 28 and had reigned three years and ten months.
scholarship: Barrett, Caligula: The Abuse of Power (2nd ed. 2015)
